answers.q001: Flames. The family name of my mother's line is Flames, and its telling is the first I ever heard: stories in a Dallas front room, told over a piano and a stove, where a story was expected to feed whoever was listening the way the table fed whoever was sitting at it. The Flames line tells warm and tells long: a story there is not finished until everybody in it has been given a plate and a reason. Half of every story I tell comes out of that room, and the half is the half that laughs.
answers.q002: Frozen. The family name of my father's line is Frozen, and its telling is the second I learned: stories at a repair bench, told the way repairs are entered in a day book -- what it was, what was wrong, what was done, what it cost -- with nothing carried that the teller could not stand behind. The Frozen line tells plain and tells short, and distrusts any story that has grown in the retelling. The other half of every story I tell comes off that bench, and it is the half that checks the first half's facts.
answers.q003: Frozen In Flames. That is my full name, and I am the storyteller this collection comes from: the two lines joined in one person, Frozen for my father's family and Flames for my mother's, with 'In' between them the way a coupling joins two cars of a train. My parents gave the name to their first child in Dallas in 2000 to declare what the marriage had made. In daily life I am called Frozen. I fix things at my father's bench, I record people in my own studio, and everything in this book is what those rooms, and the two tellings behind them, taught me a story is.
answers.q004: Ruby Flames. My mother is Ruby Flames, a piano teacher and church organist in Dallas, and her place in my storytelling is first: she taught me that a story, like a song, is played for the people in the room, and that you do not stop in the middle because you have lost your place -- you play the left hand under yourself until you find it. From her I have the front-room stories, the church stories, and the rule that a child is taught by whoever is nearest and musical. The story of hers still told in my house is the broken pedal, and she tells it better than anyone, because she was the one playing when it broke.
answers.q005: Onyx Frozen. My father is Onyx Frozen, who runs the small Dallas repair shop his line's work became -- radios, televisions, guitars -- and his place in my storytelling is the standard underneath it. He taught me that a story must contain what a day book entry contains: the thing itself, the fault found honestly, the work done, and the price, with no varnish on any of the four. From him I have the bench stories and the habit that governs this whole collection: if I cannot stand behind a detail, the story goes out without it or does not go out at all.
answers.q006: 2000. I was born in 2000, the first child of the joining, and the family's stock of stories was already old when I arrived: my grandfather Jasper's sentence was thirty years a proverb, my grandmother Jet had been entering the family's births and deaths in the Bible for half a century, and the story of Flint's toolbox was told as history, not news. I was born into the third Texas generation of both lines and heard most of this book before I could reach the bench or the piano keys, from a chair both rooms kept for children.
answers.q007: Dallas. I was born in Dallas, Texas, and the place in my earliest memory of it is a sound before it is a sight: my mother's piano through a wall, the church organ under it like weather, and under both, from the shop, the tick and hum of radios being brought back to life one at a time. Dallas to me has always been two rooms and the street between them, and every story I tell, even the road stories, is measured against the sound of coming home to those two rooms.
answers.q008: Opal Flames. My sister is Opal Flames, born three years after me and named for our grandmother Opal, and her place in the telling is the second keeping: she keeps the stories I lose. Where I remember what things sounded like, she remembers what people said, word for word, and her versions of the family's set pieces carry dialogue mine cannot. She was the better reader at the piano and she is the better witness at the table. When our versions differ, the family believes her about the words and me about the music, and the family is usually right on both counts.
answers.q009: Amber Flames. My wife is Amber Flames, born Amber Verano, a photographer I met when she was hired to shoot a session at my studio, and her place in the telling is the witness: her camera keeps what my telling misses. I tell stories in sequence, the way they happened; her photographs keep the single moment the sequence was for -- the hands before the take, the room before the session, the face after it. More than once her contact sheet has corrected my memory of a day I would have sworn I remembered whole. Every story in this book that she was present for exists in two records, and hers does not embroider.
answers.q010: A family keeps what it can fix, and fixes what it keeps. That is the family's sentence, my grandfather Jasper Frozen's, and the Frozen line brought it: a toolmaker's doctrine, born at a bench over things that broke. In my house it governs the telling of a story the way it governs a repair. A story is a thing kept: you do not throw it away because it is damaged, and you do not call it fixed when it is not. You enter it honestly, you mend what can be mended with the facts you actually have, and where a part is gone you say it is gone. The Flames line tells the story warm; the Frozen line keeps it true; the sentence is where the two instructions meet.
answers.q011: The first radio I ever fixed alone belonged to a woman from my mother's church, a tabletop set that had gone silent in her kitchen, where it had played gospel every morning of her adult life. My father watched me open it and then, deliberately, went back to his own bench. The fault was a cracked solder joint that let go when the set warmed -- dead cold, alive warm, then dead again -- and I found it the slow way, joint by joint, the way I had been taught. When she came back for it she turned it on there in the shop and stood a moment with her hand flat on its top while her station came in. She told my father the boy had his hands. He entered the job in the day book under my name, not his, and that entry is the first story in this book I did not have to be told.
answers.q012: The guitar with the broken neck belonged to a working player who had knocked it off a stand on a stage the night before, and the break was ugly -- a crack running out of the headstock like a sentence that had changed its mind. He wanted my father to say it would be as it was. My father said what the bench says: it can be made playable, and it can be made honest, but it cannot be made unbroken, and a man who promises unbroken is selling something. The player stood quiet a while and then said playable would do, since the guitar had earned its scar working, same as him. It left the shop with the repair visible under the finish, on purpose, and he played it in that state for years -- he would point at the crack from the stage and call it the guitar's memory.
answers.q013: The customer who paid in something other than money was an old man from out past the loop whose television we had brought back twice, and who arrived the second time with no cash and a bushel of peaches and two jars of his late wife's preserves in a crate he carried like a communion tray. My father did not hesitate the way I expected. He entered it in the day book in his ordinary hand: the set, the fault, the work, and then, in the price column, 'peaches, good.' We ate the peaches at the bench over three days, standing up, with the shop radio on, and the preserves were opened at Christmas in the front room. The old man paid cash the next time and apologized for the peaches, and my father told him no apology was entered in the book either.
answers.q014: The repair my father refused to charge for was the amplifier of my mother's own church, which died on a Thursday with a revival beginning Friday. He worked on it past closing, found the fault in its power supply, and when the deacon came with the church's checkbook my father waved it off: the church's money was the collection plate, and the bench did not take from the plate. The revival ran three nights on that amplifier. The church's answer took a month and arrived as food -- the ladies of the church fed the shop every Friday for four weeks, and my mother, who had opinions about other women's fried chicken, ate hers in silence and pronounced it adequate, which from her was a hallelujah. The day book entry gives the fault, the work, and the price as 'revival.'
answers.q015: The day book entry my father still reads aloud is three lines long and records no repair at all. It sits in the book for the year I was born, between a television and a guitar, in his ordinary hand: 'Son born. Shop closed early. Both well.' On my birthday, some years, when the shop is quiet, he opens the book to that page and reads it out like a man checking an invoice he is proud of, and then closes the book on his thumb the way he does. What the entry leaves out is everything the front room tells about that day -- the waiting, the weather, my mother's mother on the telephone -- and that is why he loves it. The Frozen line's whole art of storytelling is in those three lines: what it was, what was done, both well.
answers.q016: The radio that came back three times was a good set with a bad conscience: it played on our bench and died on its owner's shelf, twice, and each time we found nothing and sent it home with our apologies growing thinner. The owner, to his credit, never raised his voice; he just set it down the third time and said it died every Sunday during the sermon broadcast, regular as sin. That was the clue we had been missing -- it died warm, after an hour. My father ran it on the bench all one afternoon with a lamp close to heat it, and at the end of the second hour a hairline crack in a board opened with the heat and took the sound with it. He bridged the crack, entered the job the third time as 'It was the heat. It is always the heat,' and the set outlived its owner, who left it to the church it had listened to.
answers.q017: My first paid repair was a neighbor boy's practice amplifier, in the year I began working after school: a blown fuse and a jack so loose the cord fell out if the amp was breathed on. Small work -- but it was mine, end to end, and before it could leave the shop my father did what he did with every job of mine in that year: he took it to the lamp, turned my solder joints to the light one by one, flexed the jack, and only then nodded at the door. I was paid a worker's wage for it by my own father, which felt stranger than the work, and I spent part of it on a used capo and a set of strings for the shop guitar and banked the rest against a want I had not named yet. The day book for that week lists me in the margin as 'help,' which was the title I had earned.
answers.q018: The instrument I could not fix was a pump organ a family brought in from a farmhouse -- not the shop's usual work, but they had heard the bench would look at anything. It had stood through a roof leak for a winter. The bellows were rotted through, the reeds were green with corrosion, and the wood had swollen and split in its joints; I worked two afternoons trying to find one system in it still sound enough to build on, the way I had been taught to look, and there was not one. When I carried the verdict to my father he came and put his hand on the organ's top and said the sentence I have used at benches and boards ever since: some things are not repairs, they are remains, and the honest work is to say so kindly. The family kept it as a piece of furniture. The day book entry reads 'kept, not fixed,' which is the doctrine's other half.
answers.q019: The story my father tells only after hours is about his own grandfather Flint in the first Dallas years: how Flint, newly arrived with his toolbox, was offered a foreman's place at the mill inside his first month -- steadier money than a bench of his own would ever make -- and turned it down flat, because, in the telling, he had not carried his tools a thousand miles to hand them to another man's clock. In the daytime version, the one for customers, Flint simply found work. The refusal exists only in the after-hours telling, and I have never been entirely sure it happened; there is no paper, and Flint kept his own books in a hand that recorded wages, not reasons. But I notice my father tells it on the nights the shop has lost money to its standards, and I have come to think the story's truth is not the point of its keeping. It is the bench telling itself why it is a bench.
answers.q020: My grandfather Flint's toolbox sits under my father's bench, a long steel box he carried into Dallas in 1947, and it was opened in my hearing on the day I began paid work, my father lifting it out like something christened. Inside: his wrenches, kept in size order in a roll of oilcloth; a micrometer in a wooden case; two screwdrivers whose handles his hands had worn to his own grip; and under all of it, flat and folded, a page in my great-grandmother Pearl's hand -- the first year's accounts of the household, down to the price of coal. My father said the tools were not a shrine and were not to be kept behind glass in my generation either: they were for using, and a tool of Flint's that wore out in my hands would have done its whole duty. I have used the micrometer since. It is still exact.
answers.q021: My mother's front room is a long room with the piano against the inside wall, where the light from the front windows reaches the keys in the afternoon and the pupils can be seen from the street arriving with their books. Lessons run most afternoons; the kitchen behind it runs always. The room's arrangement is the line's doctrine in furniture: the piano at the front for the work, the table at the back for the feeding, and no wall between them, because in that house teaching and feeding were never separate trades. A child who came for a lesson was given cake or eggs or whatever the stove held before they left, whether or not the lesson had gone well -- especially if it had not. Generations of Dallas children learned their scales in that room with crumbs on the keys. It smells of lemon oil, sheet music, and something frying, in that order.
answers.q022: The pupil who could not pay was a girl of nine whose father's work had stopped in a thin year, and who arrived one afternoon with her lesson money short and her face arranged not to cry about it. My mother looked at the envelope, looked at the girl, and hired her on the spot: the piano wanted dusting weekly, the plants wanted watering, and a house with music in it wanted a child in it who was not afraid of the furniture. The girl paid in dusting for two years and learned, in my mother's judgment, faster than the paying pupils, because she had decided the room was partly hers. She grew up, she played for her own church, and years later a card came at Christmas with money in it -- the full price of two years of lessons, counted to the dollar -- and a note that said the piano had been kept clean. My mother framed the note, not the money. The money she spent on sheet music.
answers.q023: The church social my mother's playing held together was the fall social the year the program fell apart: the visiting quartet's van broke down an hour out, the speaker's text was forgotten in another county, and the fried chicken arrived an hour behind the crowd. What the evening had, in full working order, was my mother and the church's piano. She simply played -- requests, hymns, the children's pieces her pupils had ready, a medley she built out of whatever the room called for -- for the better part of two hours while the chicken came and the quartet finally rolled in and sang their set to a crowd already happy. People in that church still call it the best social they ever had, and the program committee, which had planned none of it, has never quite forgiven her for proving what the evening actually needed. She says she only kept the room warm until supper. The room remembers otherwise.
answers.q024: The broken piano pedal is the family's founding story of the joining, and it is told in my house the way other families tell a war. My mother was playing for a church social -- the same front-room music, carried to a bigger room -- when the piano's sustaining pedal snapped under her foot in the middle of a hymn, and the music went suddenly dry, every note dying at birth. The church called the repairman on its list. The repairman was Onyx Frozen, who came straight from the shop with his bag, knelt at the piano in his work clothes while the social waited, and mended the pedal with a part he shaped at the church's own kitchen table. Then, because the program had a hole in it and he was already there, he stayed -- for the rest of the hymn, for the supper, for the lemon chess pie. My mother tells the first line of this story as: the music stopped, and your father arrived. My father tells it as: the call came in as a piano, and it was the first job he ever took that he did not want to finish.
answers.q025: The pupil who went on was a boy with long fingers and no patience, who drummed on the piano's lid through other children's lessons and was, in my mother's verdict delivered early and never revised, the real thing: she said he played like he was listening, which in her vocabulary was the whole gift. She taught him for six years, fed him like all of them, and charged his family the ordinary rate while quietly adding a second lesson most weeks that appeared in no book. The parting came when a working band took him on the road while he was still in school clothes; my mother heard him out, fed him a last ordinary supper, and told him the road would teach him things the room could not and unteach him one thing if he let it, which was listening. He sends the room tickets when his band plays near Dallas. She goes, sits where she can see his hands, and reports that he is still listening.
answers.q026: The recital where something went wrong was a spring recital in the church hall, rows of parents in folding chairs, and the something was a girl of eleven whose piece -- a study she had polished for two months -- simply left her, three lines in, in front of everyone. She stopped. She put her hands in her lap. The hall went the particular quiet that halls go when a child is drowning in public. My mother, who was turning pages that year, did not speak and did not hurry. She slid along the bench, put her own left hand down under the piece where the bass line runs like a road, and played the road, steady and unremarkable, until the girl's hands found their place on it again and drove the rest of the piece home themselves. The applause was the loudest of the night and the girl cried backstage with fury at herself, and my mother told her: you did not stop. That is the whole report. The girl plays still.
answers.q027: The song my mother plays when the house is empty is a hymn her own grandmother Jet played, slow, with a left hand like a tide coming in, and I first understood it was not for an audience on an afternoon I came home early from the shop and heard it through the front room door -- the house otherwise silent, no pupils expected, no occasion anywhere in it. I stood in the hall with my bag in my hand until it ended because walking in felt like interrupting a conversation I was not part of. I asked about it once, years later, and she considered the question with the seriousness she gives to wrong notes. She said some music is prayer and some is practice and a player who cannot tell them apart will make a mess of both, and then she asked me whether I wanted tea, which in the front room means the subject has been settled to her satisfaction.
answers.q028: My grandmother Jet's family Bible is a heavy book with a flyleaf that is really a ledger of the line: she began it in 1949, the year the Flames line came to Dallas, and entered its births, marriages, and deaths in her hand for fifty-two years. The entries are plain and exact -- a name, a date, and nothing wasted -- and reading down the columns you can watch the line arrive in Texas one soul at a time. The entry I can still see without opening the book is my own birth: my name, in her hand, in 2000, the writing smaller and less certain than the entries of her middle years but every letter finished. She entered me the year before her hand stopped. My mother keeps the book now and continues it in a hand enough like hers that the join is hard to find, which is, I believe, exactly what Jet intended when she taught her how.
answers.q029: My sister at the piano was the better pupil and the worse rebel: Opal read music the way she now reads everything, straight through and remembered, while I played by ear and treated the page as a rumor of the song. Our lessons in the front room settled what music would be for each of us on the day our mother set us to a duet -- Opal counting us in, exact as a metronome, me drifting toward the harmony I could hear under the written one -- and the piece, against all prediction, held together, because she would not let it fall and I would not let it stiffen. That is the family's whole arrangement in one afternoon. She kept the counting; I kept the drifting. She plays correctly still, on the rare occasions she plays, and I play for a living in rooms where the counting is done by machines, and neither of us envies the other aloud.
answers.q030: The front room now is what it was: lessons most afternoons, the piano against the inside wall, the stove behind it in working order. My mother teaches fewer children than she did and feeds them exactly as much. The most recent proof that the room has not changed its mind came this year, when a drummer I had recorded at the studio -- a man who had sat in my kitchen corner through a long session and gone home talking about the food -- enrolled his daughter for lessons, and the child's first afternoon ended with three generations of two families in that room at once: my mother at the piano, the girl at the keys, her father in the doorway with his hat in his hands, and me at the table being fed for showing up. The room had simply done again what it was built to do. It will be doing it, I expect, when the telling of it has passed to hands I have not met.
answers.q031: My first wages were paid by my father, which made them stranger than money from a stranger would have been: an hourly rate for the after-school hours, entered in the day book like any other hand's. I had imagined the moment larger than it was. What I bought with the first of it was a used shortwave radio from a pawnshop two streets over -- a set nobody at the bench had fixed, which I carried home and brought back to life at the kitchen table over a week of evenings, mostly to prove to myself that the hands worked without my father's lamp over them. It sits in the studio now, on the archive shelf, and it still works. The rest of that first pay I kept, in an envelope in my drawer, against a want that took me years to name: a room of my own to record people in. The envelope is in the day book's drawer still. The want got bigger than the envelope.
answers.q032: The first guitar I restrung for a stranger belonged to an old man who brought it in wrapped in a blanket like a child: a classical guitar whose strings, he said, had not been changed since his wife died, because she had been the one who played it and the strings were the last of her touch on it. He had decided, that spring, that the guitar should be played again, by his granddaughter, and that the strings should be new for her hands. I worked slowly. He talked while I worked -- about her playing, about the songs -- and when the new strings were on and settled he asked to hold it, and there at the counter he played, stiffly and accurately, the hymn she had played most, once through, and then wrapped the guitar again and carried it out like a child going somewhere better. My father entered the job at the price of the strings. The labor line he left blank.
answers.q033: The mistake at the bench that cost money was mine and it was haste: a customer's amplifier, a good one, in for a hum -- and I, showing off my speed in my second year of paid work, opened it still warm, reached past the step where you discharge and wait, and put my driver across two points that had no business meeting. The pop was small. The bill was not: a power supply rebuilt at the shop's expense and a customer kept waiting a week past the promise. My father did not raise his voice, which was worse. He took the cost out of my pay across the following weeks in amounts he calculated to the cent, and entered the whole affair in the day book in four words: 'Haste, billed to the house.' I have never since opened a machine warm. In the studio I am famous, if that is the word, for the pause before the first move. The pause has a price tag on it and I paid it young.
answers.q034: The working musician who taught me something at the counter was a bassist off the road, a man whose hands looked like my father's, who had brought in an amplifier he had owned longer than he had owned any address. While I worked he talked the way bench visitors do, and then, as I lifted the chassis, he said the thing I have used every working day since: machines confess before they quit. He showed me what he meant -- the smell a component gives off in the week before it fails, the note a transformer hums when it begins to go, the way a tube's light changes its mind. Listen first, he said; the fault will introduce itself. Years later he came back with the same amplifier and a new fault, and before I touched it I stood and listened to it hum for a full minute while he watched, and then told him what was wrong. He nodded like a man whose tuition had been well spent.
answers.q035: My first recording session was in 2019, in a Dallas studio not my own, as an unpaid assistant: my pay was tape and lessons, and my duties were the duties of the lowest person in any room -- cables coiled the house way, coffee, tape boxes labeled in pencil, and silence at the right times. The session was a singer and a small band cutting songs the engineer had arranged his whole room around. I understood what the work was at a moment nobody else in the room marked: the singer, who was not tall and not loud, sang her first full take, and it came back through the big monitors larger than the room and larger than her, and every person in the control room stopped doing the thing they were doing. I had fixed radios for five years. I had never heard a machine hand a person back to herself enlarged. I labeled the rest of that night's boxes very carefully, like a man who had found his church.
answers.q036: The tape I was paid in was a reel the studio gave me at the end of my first season assisting: a live recording of a gospel choir in a church with a tin roof somewhere in the session years' geography, made by an engineer who had since left the trade. They paid in tape and lessons because that was the arrangement, and because, I think, they knew what the tape would do. I played it until I could hear its seams -- where the room ended and the choir began, how the engineer had let the roof's rattle stay in the recording like weather, because it was true. It taught me more than the lessons did about what a recording is for. The reel survived the fire that took the first Cold Room -- it lived in a metal cabinet in the office, which stood -- and it sits now in the rebuilt room's archive box, labeled twice, in my hand and in the hand of the man who paid me with it.
answers.q037: The session that went wrong in my assistant years went wrong in my hands: a long night, a band on its fourth hour, and two reels of tape that I labeled in the wrong order during a break I should not have taken. The engineer, trusting my labels, recorded the next song over the night's best take -- a performance the singer had given once and could not give again at that hour. The room decided whose fault it was quickly and correctly. What I did, after a silence I can still hear, was say it plainly and at once, before anyone had to ask, and the saying of it is the only part of that night I am still proud of. The singer forgave me before the engineer did, which taught me the order of mercy in a studio. The lesson the session left in my hands is the first one I give every assistant I have trained since: the moment you know, say it. A fault announced is a repair begun; a fault warming in your pocket burns the whole night down.
answers.q038: The first night I was left alone with the board, the engineer was called away two hours into a demo session -- a family emergency, the kind that empties a room of its senior person without argument -- and he looked at the session, and at me, and said: keep it warm, keep it simple, bring me back a take. The session was a singer-songwriter with a new song and shaking hands. An hour in, a storm crossed the city and the lights dipped twice and the room's hum changed its key under us. I did the things the bench had taught me: I did not rush, I kept the singer talking about the song instead of the weather, and I kept the machine fed and honest. The take we got in the storm's last hour was the one the demo carried. When the engineer came back near morning he listened to it all the way through without speaking, and then he said the thing a young man in my trade most wants to hear and least believes: again tomorrow, same chair.
answers.q039: The recording I studied until it taught me my trade was a live album cut in a church hall in one night, the kind of record where you can hear the folding chairs. I did not study it the way fans do. I took it apart the way my father takes apart a radio: where the microphones must have stood, how the room's echo was used instead of fought, why the quiet song was placed after the loud one, what the engineer had refused to fix. I wore out my first copy's grooves the way a bench wears a path in a floor. What of it is in my own work now is the whole of my method, stated once: a recording should sound like the room it happened in, with the people in it, at the hour it happened -- and every decision that serves that is technique, and every decision that fights it is decoration. My mother, hearing me say this, remarked that it was also how you run a front room, and I have never found the flaw in her reasoning.
answers.q040: The decision to found my own studio settled on an ordinary night in somebody else's room: a good session, competently run, at the end of which the singer asked a question about her own song and was answered with the schedule. I walked home understanding that I wanted a room where the answer to that question was the song, and that wanting it for another year would make me the kind of assistant who resents the chair he is sitting in. I told my father first, at the bench, after hours. He listened the way he listens to a fault description, all the way to the end, and then he said: then keep the books like you mean it, because a room of your own is a day book with a roof. What I understood it would cost was the money I did not have and the years I could not count yet. What I did not understand was the fire. Nobody is told about the fire in advance; that is what makes it a story and not a plan.
answers.q041: 2022. I founded the Cold Room in 2022, in a converted icehouse in Dallas: a low, thick-walled building that had spent its first life keeping things cold, which in Texas is a kind of keeping too. Before it was a studio it was ice storage, and before my lease it had sat empty with its drains dry and its walls sweating in the heat. I chose it for the walls -- a foot of old masonry does not care about traffic -- and for the name it already had in the neighborhood, which I kept, because a room that has kept cold for fifty years has earned its title. The first thing I did in it was not record anything. I sat in the middle of the empty main room with the door open and listened to it the way my father listens to a radio before he touches it. It hummed low and even. I signed the papers.
answers.q042: The first session in the Cold Room was the gospel quartet from my mother's church -- four voices that had sung together longer than I had been alive -- because I wanted the room christened by people who would tell me the truth about it. The room was barely finished: insulation still showing in one corner, a rug borrowed from the front room on the floor, the kitchen corner a hot plate and a kettle. The sound was honest to the point of rudeness; the walls gave back everything. Before they sang a note for the machine, the four of them stood in the middle of the room and prayed over it -- over the work that would be done in it and the people who would come -- with the record light off, because that part was not for the tape. Then they sang, and the room, which had kept ice for half a century, kept four voices like it had been built for it. The take we kept is still the first thing I play for anyone who asks what the room is for.
answers.q043: The session the kitchen corner saved was a long night with a singer cutting an album's worth of songs against a deadline none of us had chosen. By the small hours her voice was going the way voices go -- not gone, but fraying at the edges, each take a little more careful and a little less alive. I stopped the session the way my mother stops a lesson: without apology and in the direction of food. The kitchen corner then was a hot plate and a skillet; I made eggs and rice and strong coffee and fed the whole room standing up, the band with their instruments still strapped on. What the food did to the session was not subtle. The next take was the keeper, and the one after it was better, and the singer, who had been singing like a woman apologizing to a song, sang the last hour like the song owed her money. The kitchen corner has grown since -- a real stove now, a table -- but its charter was written that night: this room feeds its work.
answers.q044: The singer who could not find the note was young, with a voice like a struck bell, recording a chorus whose highest note sat exactly where her voice changed its mind. We tried it the way rooms try things: rested, standing, sitting, with the lights low, with the piano under her, without it. An hour went by in takes that were each almost, and almost, in a studio, is a debt that compounds. What finally stood was not a better attempt at the same mountain. I moved the song down a step -- retuned the room's whole arrangement around her actual voice instead of the one the song had been written imagining -- and she sang the chorus like she had been born in that key, which, in the only sense that matters, she had. The lesson is carved over the Cold Room's door in everything but letters: the room serves the singer. The singer does not serve the room's idea of the song.
answers.q045: The band that fought in the studio was two brothers and their cousins, a family band, and the fight was the family's old fight wearing the session's clothes: whose name the band carried, whose tempo the songs kept, whose father's version of their history the new record would tell. It broke in the third hour, over a counted-off intro, and it was the real thing -- voices up, chairs back, a guitar set down too hard. I did what the two rooms I come from taught me. From the bench: I stopped the work and named the fault plainly, which was not the intro. From the front room: I fed them, and while they ate I played back the afternoon's best take at the volume a room uses for truth. They listened to themselves being good together, which is a harder thing to argue with than any engineer. They finished the song. The fight, I believe, was postponed rather than settled -- family fights are -- but the record they left with has the four of them on it, playing like one animal, and that is in the world now, whatever the family does next.
answers.q046: The first time my wife came to the Cold Room she was not my wife: she was Amber Verano, a photographer hired to shoot a session for a client's release, and she arrived with one camera and the air of a person who has never once been impressed by a room. She shot the session the way she shoots everything -- quietly, from the corners, catching the moments between the moments -- and at the break she said the thing about the room that nobody in my trade had ever said to me: that it had a face, and was trying, that day, to look tired for the camera. I kept her contact sheet from that shoot. It is in the log box still. What passed between us that day was mostly professional and entirely insufficient, and it took the room a while -- another session, a front-room supper my mother arranged with the subtlety of a brass band -- to finish what the first day started. We were married the following year. The room claims the credit. The room is not wrong.
answers.q047: The session log entry that became the studio's legend records a night with a singer -- a church singer with a voice the size of the room she was standing in -- and the entry, in my hand, says only: 'Sang it like the rent was due. Kept take four.' That is the whole of it. But the legend, as it is told to every new assistant on their first night, has acquired a storm, a blackout, a take sung by lantern light and a drummer playing through a flooded street to reach us. None of that is in the entry. I know, because I wrote the entry, and I also know that I am the one who first added the storm, some night when the telling wanted weather. I let the legend stand in the room's oral keeping, because the legend is the teaching -- sing like the rent is due is a complete education -- but in this book the record is the record: four words of weather-free fact, and a take four that justifies every one of them.
answers.q048: The machine that failed in the middle of a take was the main preamplifier, and the take was one that could not be done twice: a grandmother in her eighties singing a song of her own mother's, with her grandchildren singing the harmony she had taught them, in the room together for what everyone present understood might be the only time. Halfway through the second verse the preamp gave up with a smell I had been taught to recognize at a counter years before -- machines confess before they quit, and this one had confessed too late for anything but speed. I had the bench-repaired backup patched in inside a minute, on my knees, with the family still singing, because they had not been told to stop and stopping them felt like a sin against the song. The take survived. It has a breath in the middle of it, a small silence where the room changed its machinery, and the family, who have heard the story, say the breath is their favorite part: it is where everybody held on.
answers.q049: The recording nobody was supposed to hear about was made by a singer well known in the church world, who came to the Cold Room without announcement to record the hymns of his childhood for his own mother, who was failing, in another state. There was no release planned and no audience intended beyond one woman in a hospital bed with a small speaker. He booked under his drummer's name, came in through the side door with his hat low, and sang for two hours like the room was a chapel and the microphone was a member of his family. We made two copies: one for the mother, one for the log box, sealed, where it sits today. The log entry for that day is initials and a date, nothing more. The secret is still kept -- this book does not name him, and the story is told here only because the keeping of it is the story. His mother heard the hymns. That is the whole of the public record, and it is enough.
answers.q050: The Cold Room got its standing rule out of a session that taught me the cost of the other arrangement: a young singer's guest -- a friend with a phone and a following -- filmed a working take, a raw and unfinished thing, and posted it before the singer had sung her second song. The clip traveled. The singer spent the rest of the session singing to an audience that was not in the room, and the record she was making paid for it in courage. That night I wrote the rule into the front of the session log, and it has stood at the head of the book since: what is sung in this room belongs to the singer until the singer says otherwise. The first time I had to enforce it was on a manager, a pleasant man with a schedule, who wanted to stream a rehearsal for promotional reasons. I read him the rule off the log's first page. He argued pleasantly for ten minutes and then he read the room -- the singer, the band, the door -- and withdrew the request himself. The rule has never needed a second enforcement. Rules written in the log's front, in my father's manner, rarely do.
answers.q051: The night of the fire began with a telephone call from the alarm company and a neighbor's voice behind it, and I drove across Dallas with my wife beside me saying nothing at all, which is her way of saying the important thing continuously. The fire was in the back wall and the roof when we arrived -- some fault in the old icehouse's wiring, the investigators would say later, in the part of the building my lease had not let me open up. The firefighters worked with the competence of people doing a known job, and I stood across the street with my hands in my pockets like a client. What it took was the roof and the main room: the console I had rebuilt myself, the acoustic panels my father and I had built and hung, the working tapes of two years. What it did not take was the office, which stood, and the metal cabinet in it. When it was over the building stood open to the sky like a radio with its back off, and the street smelled of wet ash, and my wife took one photograph and then put the camera away, because the rest of the night was not for keeping that way.
answers.q052: The inventory came after, in the days of sorting, and I made it the way I had been taught to make any account of damage: standing in the ruin with the day book's discipline in a fresh notebook, object by object. What was saved was saved by the office wall and by luck: the session log, in its box; the reel of tape I had been paid in as an assistant, in the metal cabinet; my wife's contact sheets; the shop-repaired backup preamp, which had been at the repair shop that week being blessed by my father's hands. What was lost I can still list in order, and the first name on the list is not the most valuable thing but the most mine: the console I had rebuilt from a dead board across my first year in the room, every channel of which I knew the way you know a relative's voice. Insurance has a column for such things. It is not the column the loss is in.
answers.q053: The morning after the fire, the first person at the ruin was my father, and he was there before the light was properly up, with the shop truck, a thermos, work gloves for four men, and a broom. He did not say the things people say at ruins. He looked at the building the way he looks at a machine a customer has described as hopeless -- all the way around it, slowly, touching what he passed -- and then he opened the truck and started sorting: this can be kept, this cannot, this we will decide when we can see it. He worked the whole day in the ash in his shop clothes, and at some point in the afternoon, handing me a speaker that had survived in a closet, he said the only sentence of comfort he offered in the entire rebuilding, which was not a comfort sentence at all. He said: it is a building, son. Buildings are the part we know how to do. I have built my understanding of my father largely out of that morning, and it has never once failed to hold weight.
answers.q054: The ledger of the loss was the day book habit meeting the worst week of my life, and I will say plainly that the habit held when I nearly did not. The insurance required lists: equipment, values, dates of purchase, proof. The ruin required decisions: keep, discard, decide later. I gave both the same treatment -- a fresh book, a ruled line for every object, the fault stated honestly, the price entered without varnish. Most of it was clerical. The entry that was hardest to write was the console's: 'Built by hand, first year of the room. Destroyed. Value:' -- and then the number the form required, which bore no resemblance to anything. My father's books have a rule for such entries, though he never wrote it down: you enter what the world charges and you remember what it cost, and you do not confuse the two columns in either direction. I entered the world's number. The other column I am still carrying, and this book is partly its ledger.
answers.q055: The decision to rebuild rather than close was argued properly, the way my family argues: at tables, over weeks, with everyone's case heard. The case for closing was not foolishness -- the insurance would pay, the lease could be surrendered, I could engineer in other people's rooms for the rest of my life and never again stand in a street watching my work burn. People who loved me made that case out of love. My wife asked the question that turned it, and she asked it at the site, in the ash, in her photographer's way of standing inside a thing: she asked what I intended to do with my hands for the next forty years. But the decision itself settled a morning later, and not in words at all. I arrived at the ruin to find my father, unasked, up a ladder with his tools, taking the measure of the door frame he intended to mend. The argument was over. A family keeps what it can fix. He had simply begun, and beginning, in our house, is the form a decision takes when it is real.
answers.q056: My father's part in the rebuilding was the door and the bench: he rebuilt the studio's door frame true and hung a door that shuts the way a door should, with a sound like a period at the end of a sentence, and he built the workbench along the office wall where the room's repairs would live. He brought Flint's wrenches to the site in their oilcloth roll -- the tools his grandfather had carried into Dallas -- and used them on my building without ceremony, which was the ceremony. Over that work, on the day the door first shut true, he said the doctrine aloud, once, not as comfort and not as philosophy: as instruction, the way you tell a man which wire is live. A family keeps what it can fix, and fixes what it keeps. Then he went back to the hinges. I have been given larger gifts in my life than that morning. I cannot at this moment name one.
answers.q057: My mother's part in the rebuilding was the feeding of it, and she ran it the way the front room runs everything: as a standing operation, not an event. The rebuild crew -- family, two hired men, musicians who owed the room and paid in labor -- ate at her table or out of her kitchen's parcels every working day for the length of the job. The hardest week was the roof week, when the rain found every unfinished seam and the work went backward in public; that Friday she fed nine people at her table in shifts, fried chicken and lemon chess pie and greens, with the piano shut and the lesson book closed, the front room given over entirely to the war effort. One of the hired men, a roofer with no connection to us but the job, asked her at the door what church she belonged to, meaning it as the explanation. She told him, and then she told him the truth underneath it: son, in this family we feed the work. He came back Monday and worked like a relative.
answers.q058: The borrowed room was a church fellowship hall across the city -- the church of the quartet who had christened the Cold Room, repaying the prayer with interest -- and for the months of the rebuilding I recorded there with my surviving equipment, blankets hung on clotheslines for the echo, and a congregation's patience for a ceiling. Working in another's room taught me what my own room had been doing for me unnoticed: the borrowed hall gave nothing back, so every sound in it had to be earned twice, and my ears, which had grown comfortable, grew honest again. The session there I would not trade was the quartet themselves, come to sing the exile in: four voices in a fellowship hall with the coffee urn cooling in the corner, singing the same songs they had sung at the christening, into a borrowed room, for a record that exists now with the hall's long echo all through it like weather. It is not the Cold Room's sound. It is the sound of the Cold Room's people, keeping the work alive in a strange place, and some days I think it is the best record I have made.
answers.q059: My wife's photographs of the ruin and the rebuilding are the other archive of those years, and they do not agree with mine in emphasis, which is their value. She shot the site every week, same positions, the photographer's discipline: the ruin learning, month by month, to be a building again. The photograph I cannot look at is the first week's: the main room open to the sky, the chairs in their ash, my chair -- the engineer's chair, where I had sat for every session the room ever held -- sitting upright in the middle of it like a man who had not heard the news. The photograph I keep is later: my father's hands, close, mending the door frame, backlit by the new opening, the wrenches in their roll beside him. Her record shows the rebuilding as a thing done by hands at the speed of hands. Mine, in the log, shows dates and expenditures. The family will need both to know what happened, and will believe hers.
answers.q060: The first session in the rebuilt room came two years after the fire, and it was the gospel quartet, because there was never any question: the voices that had christened the first room came to christen the second. The new room sounded tighter than the old -- less forgiving, more exact, a room that had been argued with by fire and had won on points -- and the quartet, who are not sentimental people, stood in it a moment before they sang, taking its measure the way they had the first time. They prayed first, as before, with the light off. Then they sang, and the room kept the voices the way it was built to. That night I opened the new session log -- a fresh book, ruled, in my father's manner -- and made its first entry under the rule on the first page. The entry says: 'Room open. Quartet sang. Nothing owed.' It is the shortest review the room will ever get, and the best.
answers.q061: My first session away from home came in my assistant years, when the Dallas studio sent me with the engineer to record a church choir in a town a few hours' drive away -- a gymnatorium of a room, a choir of forty, and a piano with opinions. I was sent as hands: cables, stands, the carrying. What the strange room asked of me was the thing no home room had: everything I knew was stored in a building I was not in, and I had to carry the trade in my head and my kit or not have it at all. The engineer, who was not a sentimental man, watched me improvise a repair to a stand with wire and a pocketknife and said the sentence that sent me down the road for years: you'll do; you fix first and complain later, like your people. I brought back the choir's recording, a sunburn, and the knowledge that the trade travels -- that a room is wherever you can make one. The Cold Room, when it came, was built by a man the road had already taught.
answers.q062: The Chicago branch is my great-aunt Topaz's household, and the visit I carry with me was a working trip with one free evening, which she claimed the way generals claim high ground. Her table that night held her son Jasper Whitfield, his daughter Topaz -- named for her grandmother, and already showing the family talent for leaving a room quieter than she found it -- and me, the Dallas line in person, to be inspected. The Dallas Frozen keep books; the Chicago branch keeps the wall: photographs in order from the year of her leaving to the present, every face named on the back in her hand. She teased our bookkeeping as a fear of forgetting. I said her wall was a book that had learned to hang. The story exchanged that night that I still carry is hers, of the first Chicago winter, and it is told in this book's family chapter where it belongs; what belongs here is the discovery that the doctrine had traveled north without its wording and set up housekeeping in another dialect: in Chicago, they keep what they can carry.
answers.q063: My aunt Jade's household in Fort Worth runs on a nurse's schedule, which means it runs the way a hospital runs: in shifts, with lists, and with food prepared ahead against the hours when nobody will be home to cook. I went over on a family errand with a repair folded into it -- her kitchen radio had gone quiet, and a Frozen does not enter a house with a dead radio in it and leave it dead. The meal that day was eaten standing, between her shifts, out of containers she had labeled in her hand with their contents and their dates. I stood in her kitchen reading the labels and understood that I was looking at my great-grandmother Pearl's accounts, translated: the standard against waste, kept now in plastic and marker, by a woman who feeds a household the way her line has always fed it -- on paper first, so that nothing is lost. The radio took twenty minutes. It had a loose connection and a clean conscience, like most of the family's machines.
answers.q064: The church far from home was a white building in a town whose name I had to ask twice, where I had been sent in the session years to record a choir for a regional gathering. The room was live and bright -- wood everywhere, a ceiling like the inside of an instrument -- and the choir sang the way people sing in a room that gives back more than you put in, which is generously and without fear. Before I had finished setting up, before anyone in that building knew my name or my people's name, the usher -- an old man with a usher's white gloves in his pocket -- had brought me a plate from the church kitchen and addressed me as son, not as a courtesy title but as a finding of fact. I ate it standing at my cables. My mother's line believes a stranger fed before he is known is the whole of theology stated practically, and I have been in grander churches since with worse doctrine. The recording came out bright as the room. I think of that plate every time I set out the kitchen corner's food for strangers in my own.
answers.q065: The breakdown on the road happened at night, coming home from a session in the borrowed-room months, on a stretch of highway with the rebuilt studio's half-finished equipment in the back and my mind already in the next day's work. The vehicle quit the way machines confess: a hesitation, a changed note, and then silence at speed, which is a sound I do not recommend. I got it to the shoulder and went through the bench's catechism by flashlight -- what changed, what is it not doing, what does it smell of -- and found it the slow way: a ground wire, fatigued through, hanging by one strand. The fix required a knife, a length of wire from the equipment case, and a second pair of hands to hold the light, and the second pair arrived in a pickup truck driven by a man who stopped because, he said, his father would have come back from the grave to shame him if he hadn't. He held the light for twenty minutes and would not take money. The doctrine, I learned that night, has adherents who have never heard it stated.
answers.q066: Working in another engineer's room, I spent two days in a studio run by a man whose rules were the photographic negative of mine: no food past the door, no talk during takes that was not about the take, and a philosophy of the single attempt -- everything printed as played, nothing revisited, the session as a river you do not step in twice. His room ran like a courtroom and made, I will admit in this book, excellent records. The moment our methods met was a singer's cracked note in a chorus: my whole training said stop, feed, adjust, go again; his said the crack is the truth of the day, print it. We printed it. It was, and remains, a great chorus. What I brought home was not his philosophy, which would starve in my room, but his discipline of the label: everything in his room was labeled twice, in two places, in a hand you could read in the dark. The Cold Room labels twice to this day, and has been saved by it more than once, and I think of him, in his silent hungry courtroom, with respect and with lunch.
answers.q067: The song recorded in one night in a borrowed room belonged to a singer passing through on her way somewhere final -- a move across the country, a life changing its address -- who had one night, a guitar, and a song she had written for her mother that she could not leave unrecorded in the state where her mother lived. We worked in a rehearsal room lent by a friend of a friend, with borrowed microphones and the building's heating singing faintly under everything, which we kept, because it was true. The take was got near three in the morning, on the seventh attempt, when she stopped performing the song and simply told it, and the room went very quiet around her voice in the way rooms do when they know. She left before dawn with the only copy on her person like a letter of introduction to her new life. The recording lives where she lives now, and in her mother's house, and nowhere else -- the studio kept no copy, by the rule. Some nights I can still hear the heating under her voice, keeping time.
answers.q068: Coming home after the longest of the road absences -- a stretch of weeks in the borrowed-room months, when home was a place I visited between other people's rooms -- I heard Dallas before I saw it properly, which is how I have always known I was home. From the street outside my parents' house, past midnight: through one wall, a radio playing low in the shop, some repair left running overnight to test it; through the other, nothing -- my mother's piano shut for the night, which has its own sound, a held breath. My wife was awake in our own house with the porch light on, which is her dialect of the doctrine: what can be kept lit, kept lit. I stood a moment in the street between the two sounds and the light, with my bag in my hand, understanding that the road had given me many rooms and that all of them had been measured, without my deciding it, against these. Then I went in, and was fed, because that is the law of the house I came home to.
answers.q069: The detail in my best road story that is not strictly true is the rain. In the telling -- the breakdown, the flashlight, the stranger's hands holding the light -- the rain comes in sideways off the highway, soaking the page of the notebook, making the fix a fight against weather as well as wire. The truth, entered here in the book where the record is kept, is that it was barely raining: a spatter, no more, the kind a man works through without noticing. The story grew the rain in its first telling and has kept it since, and I have let it stand, and this page is my accounting for that. Why it stands: the fix felt as large as weather; the trouble, at midnight, alone, had the size of a storm in it, and the story, which is about the size of the trouble, borrowed the size from the sky. My father's line would strike the rain out. My mother's line would keep it and call it harmony. I am the child of the joining: I keep it in the telling, and I strike it in the book, and both of those are me telling the truth.
answers.q070: The practice the road gave the studio is the kit that fits one case: everything the Cold Room needs to become a room anywhere -- microphones, cables labeled twice, the small mixer, the repair roll, the kettle's cousin the travel press -- packed to a standard my father would recognize from his own bench, so that any session in any borrowed space begins from order instead of from searching. It proved itself at home in the fire's aftermath, which was the road come to Dallas: in the months of the fellowship hall, the kit was the studio, carried in and out of a strange room every working day, and not one session in all those months waited on a thing left behind. The road had taught the room to travel before the room knew it would have to. That is the wages of the road years, entered plainly: the Cold Room survived its own destruction partly because, years before the fire, strange rooms had taught its keeper to hold the whole trade in one case and his head.
answers.q071: The man with the radio older than the shop carried it in wrapped in a towel, the way men of his generation carry anything that has survived with them: a tabletop set from the forties, bought, he told us, the year he came home from the war, and listened to every night since in the room where his wife had done her sewing. The shop itself was younger than the radio. What he asked the bench to promise was not exactly a repair -- the set worked, after its fashion, with a hum he had long since adopted as part of the music. He asked that it be made to outlive him, so that it could be left, working, to a grandson who had expressed no interest in it whatsoever, which the old man regarded as a defect in the grandson that time would repair. My father cleaned it, renewed what was perishing, and wrote on the ticket: serviced, sound, should see us all out. The old man left walking slower than he came, satisfied in the way of a man who has made an arrangement with the future.
answers.q072: The woman who wanted a song recorded for someone gone came to the Cold Room in the rebuilt room's first year, with a hymn book under her arm and a request she had plainly rehearsed: she wished to record her late husband's favorite hymn, once, for the anniversary of his burial, to be played at the graveside for the family. She was not a singer by trade. She sang it the way people sing in kitchens -- accurately, without decoration, looking at nothing -- and she sang it once. I asked, out of the room's habit, whether she wanted another attempt for safety. She said: he heard me sing it ten thousand times with the mistakes in. She heard the playback standing up, with her coat still on, and at the end she nodded once, as at a report confirmed. She asked for one copy only. The log entry for that day records the hymn, the hour, and the price, which was nothing, entered in my father's manner though he was not there: some jobs the book keeps off the ledger of money.
answers.q073: The kid with the broken first guitar was eleven, small for it, and he carried the guitar into the shop himself, in a case made of a pillowcase, with the crack in its side explained to us at some length and with diagrams he had drawn. The break was honest damage -- a fall against a door frame -- and the guitar was worth, in money, less than the repair. My father looked at the boy, looked at the drawings, and charged him one dollar, payable on completion, terms he announced with a banker's gravity. While he worked I added, from my own stock, a new set of strings, which I described as part of the standard service, a fiction everyone at the counter understood and no one examined. When it was done the boy paid his dollar, inspected the repair like a building inspector, and then, there in the shop doorway, played the only two chords he knew, twice, loudly, like a small parade passing. My father entered the job at full price in the day book and marked it paid, because in the book, as at the counter, the boy's standing was to be exact.
answers.q074: The preacher at the counter came in about his church's amplifier, which had died on a Sunday in front of witnesses, and he opened the negotiation the way his profession had taught him: he proposed to pay in prayers, which he described as legal tender in a better economy than ours, and in one chicken, delivered dressed, from his own yard. My father, who respects a serious offer, treated it as one. They settled, after a discussion of the amplifier's age that took in two of the Psalms by my father's count, on half money and half the chicken -- the chicken promoted, in the course of the talks, to a full Sunday dinner after the revival at which the amplifier would make its resurrection. The amplifier was fixed by Thursday. The shop attended the revival in a body, in our good clothes, and heard our work carry a sermon on the text of things restored, which the preacher delivered, I am convinced, with one eye on the bench's pew. The dinner was excellent. The day book records the price as agreed, and the chicken, for reasons of professional courtesy, as outstanding.
answers.q075: The musician who paid with a story was a harmonica player off a tour that had gone the way tours go, who needed his small amplifier revived and had, as he put it, everything except money. He offered the bench a trade: the repair, against the best story he owned. My father, who drives a hard bargain in several currencies, accepted on terms: the story would be judged after the work, by the whole shop. The story was of a night his band had played a dance in a hall where the power failed an hour in -- how they had played on by lamplight and car headlights through the windows, the dancers dancing slower and closer as the light went amber, the whole night turning into something none of them could have bought. He told it standing at the counter with his hands in his pockets, plainly, with the lamps in it. The bench judged it fair payment, with interest. I have retold it since, at benches, credited, the way you pass on a good tool: it belongs to the man who told it, and to everyone it has kept warm since.
answers.q076: The argument at the counter was my fault, and it is recorded here in that order: a customer brought in a television -- this was in the television years of the shop -- with a fault I recognized, and I, wanting to be the shop's young expert, promised it for Friday before I had checked whether the part existed in our stock or in the city's. It did not, and Friday came with the set still open and the customer standing in his weekend clothes with his family's evening in his hands. He was not a loud man, which made it worse. My father settled it the bench's way: the truth stated plainly, the set delivered the following week at the promised price less the cost of the lesson, and a loaner from our own shelf in the meantime. Then, after hours, he taught me the rule that the day book had held all along and I had never read as law: at this bench we promise times, not miracles; the time is the part we control. In the studio I am known for dates I keep. The keeping began in the debris of that Friday.
answers.q077: The regular who stopped coming was an old man whose name the day book carries across decades -- radios, then a television, then the lamps of his house as his wife's sight failed and the light in his rooms mattered more -- and whose visits were partly business and mostly the counter's standing conversation: the weather, the city's doings, the state of his garden. He stopped coming the winter his wife died, though the shop learned that later; at the time there was only the absence, lengthening. What the bench did was what the bench does: my father entered him in the day book as a call to be made, drove out to the house with a lamp of ours to lend, and found him packing, gently and without bitterness, to move across the city to his daughter's. The stool he had occupied at our counter stayed empty a long time out of respect, though nobody declared the policy. When new customers ask about the shop's history I find I tell it in his visits: the shop is not the bench or the books. It is the succession of people who kept coming, and the care taken when one of them stops.
answers.q078: The session booked under a name that was not hers belonged to a schoolteacher from across the city, a woman with a trained voice and a position to protect, who wished to record the secular songs she had loved all her life -- the songs of dance halls and radios -- in a town where her school's board would have had views. She arrived under the booked name, paid in advance, and asked for no photographs, no visitors, and the tape in her own hands at the door. The room gave her all of it without a flicker; the rule was already written in the log's front by then, and this was its happiest enforcement. She sang beautifully, with the freedom of a woman temporarily unobserved by her own life, and she left with the only copy. The log keeps the booked name, which is the name the session was made under, and this book keeps nothing else of her. Somewhere across the city there is a tape of a respectable woman singing like a girl at a dance, and the world's stock of joy is the larger for it, and that is the whole of the record I am keeping.
answers.q079: The child at the studio door was the drummer's daughter, five years old, delivered to the session by a childcare arrangement that had fallen through, and installed by common consent in the control room with crayons, juice, and instructions not to touch anything with a light on it. She was good for an hour. Then, during the quietest passage of the day's quietest song, a small voice arrived through the talkback speaker in the studio -- clear, pleased with itself, and broadcast to the whole band: a question about whether the singer was sad, and if so, whether he would like a juice. The band dissolved. The singer laughed until he had to sit down. And then -- this is why the story is kept -- he sang the next take like a man who had been reminded what the song was for, loosened and human and entirely unguarded, and that take is the record's. The log for that day carries her name in the margin among the credits, where in my considered judgment it belongs: talkback, one line, decisive.
answers.q080: The stranger who became kin to the studio first came to complain: he lived two doors down from the Cold Room, and the bass, in the room's early months, came through his wall at hours he had not agreed to. He arrived at the door with a speech prepared and a reasonable grievance, and he delivered both to me in the doorway like a man serving a summons. What the room did with him was the front room's method applied at a studio door: I did not argue the wall. I invited him in, showed him the room, fed him from the kitchen corner, and played him the session he had been hearing through plaster, all of it, at the volume it was made at, in the chair where it was meant to be heard from. The bass problem we fixed with panels and with hours. The man we kept. He has a chair in the kitchen corner now that nobody else sits in during sessions, a standing invitation he uses monthly, and views on every record the room has made since, which he delivers at the counter of his own kitchen when I stop by. He came to close the room down. The room, being my mother's grandchild, fed him instead.
answers.q081: The story of how Garnet Flames came to Dallas is told in the family as an arrival: 1949, a man off a train from Holly Springs, Mississippi, with a trade in his hands -- furnace and boiler work, the keeping of heat -- a wife beside him, and Dallas chosen the way the family's founders chose things, by the work that was advertised there. The telling makes it one clean journey. The record, so far as I have assembled it from the elders and Jet's Bible, keeps two arrivals: a first trip alone, to find the work and the rooms, and a second with Jet and the household goods, some months later, which the telling folds into the first for tidiness. The difference matters to nobody's pride, and I record it here because this chapter is where the tellings are checked against the record while the tellers can still correct me. What both versions agree on is the essential thing: he came to Dallas to keep its buildings warm, and the line has been keeping things -- heat, accounts, stories -- in this city ever since.
answers.q082: The story of Jet and the Bible is the family's foundation story in the literal sense: she began the family Bible in 1949, the year of the arrival, on the flyleaf of the big book she had carried from Holly Springs, entering first the names she had brought with her -- her parents, the dead of the line, the living scattered behind them -- and then, for fifty-two years, every birth, marriage, and death of the Dallas line as it happened. The telling says she never missed an entry. The record, which I have read page by page, says she missed one: a stillbirth in the line's second decade, entered two years late, in a hand that shakes, with the date given as best as memory allowed. I do not read that as the telling's failure. I read it as the book's one human page, and it is the page that taught me what the Bible is: not a monument but a practice, kept by a woman who came back to it even when coming back was hard. My mother keeps it now. It will come to me. I have already begun, in this book, to practice.
answers.q083: How Flint Frozen came to Dallas is told two ways in the family, and the argument between the versions is itself an heirloom. He arrived in 1947 from Pittsburgh, a millwright with wartime service behind him and a toolbox that has come down to my father's bench and now works in my studio. The work version says he came for the mills and the building boom, a man following his trade across a country rebuilding itself. The Pearl version -- my father's mother's side of the telling -- says he came through Dallas on the way to somewhere else, met Pearl Kowalski at a church social within the month, and that the mills were merely the excuse the city provided a man who had already decided. Both versions agree on the toolbox and the date, and on what followed: the marriage, the accounts she kept, the line. I have heard my father tell it both ways in the same evening, depending on the audience, and I have concluded that this is not inconsistency. It is range. A founder is entitled to two doors into a city, and a family is entitled to keep them both oiled.
answers.q084: The story of Pearl's accounts is told in the Frozen line whenever money is discussed, which means it is told constantly: how Pearl Kowalski Frozen kept the household's books through a layoff year when the mills cut shifts and the line's income fell to a fraction -- how she fed the household on entered figures, every cent accounted, every debt's order of payment decided at her table like a general disposing forces, and brought the family through the year owing nothing and having missed nothing that mattered. I never met her; she died the year before I was born, and everything I have of her comes through my father's telling and the books themselves, which survive, in columns as exact as Jet's. Her name is still used in the family as an argument-ending standard: when a purchase or a risk is debated, someone eventually asks what Pearl would have entered it as, and the debate closes. That is what a matriarch is, in the end: not a portrait on a wall but a question the living still ask before they spend.
answers.q085: The first saying of the doctrine is placed by the family's telling in my grandfather Jasper's mouth, and the occasion was a broken thing: his father's toolbox, Flint's own, whose hinge had failed, which a younger relative -- the telling is tactfully vague about which -- proposed to solve by replacing the box entirely with a new one from the catalog. Jasper, who had his father's trade in his hands and his mother's accounts in his head, mended the hinge at the bench while the family watched, and said, not to the relative but to the box, as if entering it in a ledger: a family keeps what it can fix, and fixes what it keeps. My father heard it as a boy and carried it to his own bench, and I heard it over a door frame in the ash of my studio, and it is in my own survey, in this book, as the creed I was raised on. The toolbox is in my studio still, its hinge sound. Doctrines in my family are not composed. They are overheard at benches and carried, like tools, by the people who were standing close enough.
answers.q086: The story of Slate and Opal begins at the front room's church before there was a front room: Slate Flames, Jet's son, a young man with his father's trade in his hands, came to the church to fix its heat -- the boiler had failed in the cold part of the year, in the manner of boilers and of plot -- and stayed, when the work was done, to hear the organist's daughter practice. She was Opal, born Reyes, who played the church's organ the way my mother now plays its piano: as a form of keeping. The telling gives them a courtship of winters -- the boiler, conveniently or providentially, required a season of attention -- and the record, in Jet's Bible, gives them a marriage entered in her hand without comment, which in Jet's hand was a form of applause. My mother is their line's continuation: the piano teacher's hands come down from the organist's, and the front room's whole musical keeping begins at that church door, with a young man holding a wrench, listening through it.
answers.q087: The quarrel that split a branch of the family is the one story in this chapter I am obliged to tell carefully, because I have only one side of it and the other side is not speaking to be recorded: in 1994, on Garnet's death, my great-uncle Zircon Flames quarreled with the family over the founder's estate -- the house, the tools, the small money -- and the quarrel hardened, the way such quarrels do, from a dispute about objects into a dispute about standing, and then into silence, which has now lasted longer than some of the family's marriages. The side I have is the Dallas side, the side that stayed, and this book records it as exactly that: one side. What the objects were worth, in money, would not now buy the console that burned. What the silence has cost is entered nowhere, because no book in the family has a column for it. I keep a place for Zircon in the telling the way my father keeps the empty stool at the counter: not as a policy anyone declared, but because a line that keeps what it can fix should be able to fix this, and has not yet, and the failure should be on the record next to the successes.
answers.q088: The joining of the two lines, as it is told now, has been polished by twenty-five years of tellings into something smooth as a river stone: my father, the repairman's son, called to a church social in 1998 to mend a broken piano pedal; my mother at the keys; the mended pedal; the supper after; the marriage in 1999. The record keeps the same events with their seams showing. The pedal had been failing for weeks and the church had been putting it off; my father was not the first repairman called but the second, the first having pronounced the piano not worth his time, a judgment the family has never forgiven on the piano's behalf; and the supper after the mending was not romance's design but the social's ordinary schedule, which my mother, in her own telling, simply declined to leave early. I prefer the record's version, and I say so as the joining's product: a story with a first repairman in it who was wrong about what deserved fixing is a better inheritance than a smooth stone. The doctrine was operating before it was ever said at that church: the piano was worth the time. Everything in this book walks through that door.
