answers.q089: The leaving that the family re-told is my great-aunt Topaz's: in 1969 she left Dallas for Chicago, a young woman of the Frozen line going north for work and for room to be herself in, and the family's first telling of it -- the telling I heard as a boy -- was a desertion story, told with the particular relish families keep for the relative who got away. The telling has changed as the tellers aged, and the version I record here, which is the family's present one and hers, is a founding: she went north and built the Chicago branch, kept the line's standard in another dialect, raised Jasper Whitfield and the line that hangs its history on a wall. The difference between the two tellings is not evidence; the letters and the visits were there all along. The difference is the tellers, who got old enough to understand what she had done, because some of them had by then done versions of it themselves. Stories in a family are revised the way books are kept: continuously, and toward the truth, if the keepers are honest. I have tried to be honest. Her chapter of the wall, when I stood before it, was longer than the Dallas book's account of her, and better lit.
answers.q090: The two versions of the family's favorite story concern my parents' wedding feast, and they diverge on the question of what the day taught the two lines. The Flames version, told at my mother's table, holds that the feast was the day the Frozen line learned generosity: the Flames fed the whole joining -- both lines, the church, the street, it grows with the telling -- and the Frozen, who had come with their accounts in order, learned that a table is also a ledger and some entries are made in chicken. The Frozen version, told at my father's bench, holds the reverse: that the feast was the day the Flames line learned order -- that the Frozen brought the lists, the seating, the accounting of the gifts, and taught a family of feeders that keeping is also a form of love. I have heard both versions at every family gathering of my life, sometimes in the same hour, and I stand between them as their living punctuation. Both are true, which is the family's deepest doctrine and the one it has never bothered to state: a joining is not a merger. It is two keepings, kept, under one roof, arguing happily forever about whose keeping saved the day.
answers.q091: The story I have been keeping for the end is my grandfather Jasper's last visit to the bench, in the year he died. He was old and much reduced from the man who had mended Flint's toolbox hinge, and he came to the shop in my father's truck, riding the way old men ride, with his hands folded on his knees, and he asked -- not requested, asked, which in him was a ceremony -- to see my work. I was on a guitar amplifier that week, a good one, and I brought it to him and opened it and showed him the repair the way I had been taught to show work: without salesmanship. He looked a long time. He put one hand, which shook slightly, on the chassis, the way you rest a hand on a horse. Then he said: your solder is cleaner than your father's. Don't tell him; it would go to his head. It is a small story and I have kept it out of the shop's telling and the family's telling both, because some stories are a man's own wages. It is told here because this book is where the family keeps its stories, and the studio is for other people's, and this one is ours.
answers.q092: My sister's version of the family differs from mine in its evidence, and I record the difference as a finding of this book: Opal keeps what people said. Her memory is a transcript -- who promised what at which table, the exact words of my mother's ruling on any dispute, the preacher's phrases, the customers' greetings -- where mine is a recording: I keep what things sounded like, the hum of the fault, the note the room changed under a voice. Put us at the same family event and we will bring home two archives that barely overlap and are both true. Her telling of the pedal story is better than mine and she knows it: she has our parents' actual words from that evening, collected over years of asking at the right moments, where I have only the piano's make and the pedal's mechanism. When this book is argued with -- and it will be, at her table first -- her version is the one the family will send for, and they will be right to. A keeper should know the limits of his own keeping. Mine is sound. Hers is speech. The family, characteristically, kept both.
answers.q093: The photograph my wife took that says what my words cannot is of the rebuilt Cold Room in its first week -- the room finished, the equipment in, the paint dry -- taken from the door at the hour when the new window gives the room its light. There is one chair in the frame: the engineer's chair, new, bought to replace the one the fire took, sitting empty in the middle of the room facing the speakers. My words for that week, in the log and in letters, call the room finished, restored, complete -- the vocabulary of a man closing an account. Her photograph shows the truth my words were avoiding: the room is not finished. It is waiting. It has the patience of a place that knows the work will come back to it, and the chair is not a monument but an invitation. I have the print in the log box. When I am asked how the rebuilding ended, I find I no longer answer with the dates. I describe her photograph, and let the room be waiting, which is what rooms, and families, mostly are.
answers.q094: The story where the doctrine was tested hardest is the console. After the fire, the sensible course -- the insurer's course, the course every advisor recommended -- was a new console, bought whole, warranted, better on paper than the one that burned. I priced it. I sat with the catalog the way a man sits with a letter he does not want to answer. And then I did the other thing: I bought a dead board of the same family as the lost one, from a studio closing in another state, and rebuilt it by hand across the rebuilding's second year -- channel by channel, evenings, with my father's lamp over the bench and his wrenches in their roll beside me -- until the rebuilt room opened with a console that my hands knew the way they had known the first. It cost more hours than the new one would have cost dollars, and the hours were the point. A family keeps what it can fix, and fixes what it keeps: I had not understood, before the fire, that the sentence would ever be addressed to me, in a ruin, with my name on it. The console in the rebuilt room is not the best console I could have had. It is the one that is mine, which in the doctrine's accounting is the same entry.
answers.q095: The last session before the fire was a young singer -- a songwriter of nineteen, working a job in a kitchen and writing songs on the backs of order tickets -- who came in for one evening to record a song she had written for her grandmother, who was raising her and who had never heard it. The session was unremarkable in every way except the song, which was good, and her singing of it, which was better. She left with her copy, as the rule provides, and the studio's copy went into the archive that burned three weeks later. I thought about that song in the ruin more than I thought about equipment: the room's whole purpose, kept in one evening's work, ash. Then, in the rebuilding's first year, an envelope came to the shop addressed to the studio, and in it was her copy, lent back to us with a note: for the new archive, first entry, so the room starts with a song in it. It is in the rebuilt room's archive box now, ahead of the gospel tape, by her instruction and my gratitude. The rule says what is sung in the room belongs to the singer. The singer, in this case, gave some of it back, and the room began again the way it had begun: with somebody else's song, kept.
answers.q096: A story I no longer tell is the one about the famous singer at the studio: the night, in the Cold Room's first year, when a singer whose name everyone knows was said to have come in late, unannounced, and sung one song into the room's microphones before vanishing into the Dallas night. I told it for a year. It was told to me by a client, with detail and conviction, and it did the studio good in the telling, and I did not check it, because I did not want to. When I finally did the checking -- the log, the dates, the man's own touring record -- the story was not true. It had never happened. He had never been in the room. I retired the story the day I confirmed it, and I tell its retirement here because a collection of stories owes its readers its standards: a story you cannot stand behind is not an asset, it is a debt, and it compounds. The studio's real history -- the quartet, the grandmother, the singer with the bus at dawn -- needs no borrowed glory. I keep the log. The log is enough.
answers.q097: The story I tell beginners is the mislabeled tape -- my own worst night as an assistant, the best take of a session recorded over because my labels lied -- and I tell it whole, with myself as its fool, because a beginner does not need my triumphs; a beginner needs to know that the man teaching him has been the problem in the room and survived it by the only method that works, which is saying it the moment you know. I told it most recently this spring, to an assistant on his first night in the rebuilt Cold Room, a young man with good ears and shaking hands, and I watched it do for him what it was designed to do: not frighten him -- settle him. His hands steadied as the story's fool turned out to be the room's keeper. The story ends, as I tell it, with the singer's forgiveness arriving before the engineer's, and with the rule the night installed: a fault announced is a repair begun. He has since announced two faults of his own, promptly, in my hearing, and I have promoted him in my mind both times. The story is doing its work in a third generation of hands now. That is what stories in a trade are for.
answers.q098: The stories that are not mine to tell are kept under the same rule as the room's: what is sung in the Cold Room belongs to the singer, and what is told to a keeper in confidence belongs to the teller. The hardest of them to keep is a song a man recorded in my room, in the rebuilt room's first year, for a child he was not permitted to see -- a birthday song, sung by a father doing his best to be present in the only tense available to him. The tape is in the archive, sealed, labeled with a date and nothing else. Whether it was ever played for the child I do not know and will not ask; the asking would make the keeping about me. This book records that the song exists and that it is not mine, and nothing more, and I am aware that even that much is a border walked carefully. Some of the family's stories are like it: kept in sealed envelopes in the day book's drawer, their existence acknowledged, their contents the property of the living people they belong to. A collection that told everything it knew would not be a keeping. It would be a sale.
answers.q099: What this collection is for, tested against the whole of it, is the thing the doctrine has been saying all along in its workshop dialect: a family keeps what it can fix -- and a family is kept, in the end, by its tellings. The radios die and are mended and die finally; the shop will pass; the Cold Room will pass, as its first self passed, in fire or in time. What carries the line is the entered record and the told story, the Bible and the day book and the session log, and now this book, which is all three of those wearing a new coat. If it has a use for a reader outside the family, I hope it is a practical one: to send them to their own day book while the tellers of their own line still live -- to the grandmother's kitchen, the father's bench, the aunt's wall of photographs -- with a notebook and the five questions that open every story in this collection: who, what, when, where, and how. The stories are perishable. The telling is the keeping. Everything else I know is commentary.
answers.q100: The final story is the first one, told whole and plain, as it deserves: in 1998, at a church social in Dallas, the piano's pedal failed under my mother's hands in the middle of a hymn -- the piano being old, the pedal's mechanism worn, the failure a small mechanical sigh in the middle of the music. The church's first repairman had already declined the piano as not worth his time. The second man called was Onyx Frozen, the repairman's son, who came with his tools, got down on the floor in his good clothes, and mended the pedal where it lay, because the music was waiting and the room was full. My mother played the rest of the social on the mended pedal. There was a supper after, which she declined to leave early. They were married in 1999, at the same church, with the same piano played at the wedding by the bride herself, on the pedal the groom had fixed. Everything in this book descends from that evening: the front room, the bench, the Cold Room, the fire and the rebuilding, the sister, the wife, the teller. A broken thing was fixed, and a table was set, and a family -- two families, two keepings -- began. That is the whole story. It is also, the family maintains, the whole of every story: something broke, somebody stayed to fix it, and there was supper. The book is closed. The keeping goes on.
